Sisters of Code
About
Sisters of Code is the first female coding club in Cambodia that was launched by
IT Academy STEP Cambodia
in early 2019 with an aim to provide after-school digital skills training for female students from 10 to 25 y.o. During 14-18 weeks programs, female students meet every week with their trainers, all of whom are female, to learn the secrets of coding and other essential digital skills, work on projects and present their works in the teams. This is a unique non-profit educational program, that gives a never existed before opportunity for girls to explore digital skills in a supportive and encouraging environment.
​
Our Mission
Our Vision
By empowerment and support through education and confidence development, help girls and women to become active creators in the digital economy and discover their full potential.
Technology should not be a privilege,  but an equal opportunity!
Our Mission
To grow confidence among female students and share the joy of learning coding skills, empowering for a successful digital future.
​
​
Why is Sisters of Code created?
The field of technology in Cambodia is male-dominated and female students feel unwelcome in this predominantly male field. Only 30% of graduate students are enrolled in STEM-related majors, and among tertiary STEM enrollments, just 14% are women compared to 86% men. Lack of role models, lack of confidence and opportunities, pressure from society holds back female students from learning important digital skills and getting actively involved in the digital economy.
​
How can we help?
Sisters of Code exists to empower and support female students through education to discover their full potential and grow a new generation of digital creators. Our work helps girls grow confidence and challenges long-held gender stereotypes. This engagement would not only benefit girls, but also the whole society building its own equality and mutual respect principles.
We believe that by supporting girls in learning digital skills we are changing their future:
by opening new opportunities
growing students' confidence
creating a positive experience that otherwise would not be available.
Sisters of Code aims at creating a supportive environment for the girls, who wish to learn new digital skills, develop creativity and get an in-depth understanding of computer science.
​
What is our impact?
Our impact is real - 96% of Sisters of Code graduates admitted that studying coding skills was a useful or a very useful experience for them and 100% of Sisters of Code graduates would recommend other girls to join the club.
By offering this free educational program, we bring real solutions to the identified challenges, which were mentioned by the students of Sisters of Code:
46% of girls said that they are not supported to study technology or even not allowed in many cases.
27% mentioned that there are no other places for girls to study digital skills.
We believe that in order to support the economic development of the Kingdom of Cambodia, education is the key. By ensuring innovative, skills-focused, and inclusive educational programs, as well as growing interest in technology among female students, we directly contribute to the country's development.
Sisters of Code program is for impact. Impact for those who need that the most. Sisters of Code is an opportunity for girls that has not ever existed before.
We are proud that our program received 4 international awards in skills development for women and girls and we are dedicated to delivering the impact to more girls!

Meet the Team
Mrs. Natalja RODIONOVA
, Director of Sisters of Code
In Cambodia, too many girls still grow up being told to stay small, to be careful, to be modest, to choose the safe and well-known path. Sisters of Code exists to open doors to the world of technology, the world of the future. We’ve seen what happens when a girl is given something she is too rarely given: a real chance. A place where she is not judged for what she doesn’t know, but respected for her courage to learn. And once that door opens, something changes, she stops asking for permission and starts believing in her own future. They gain confidence, they shine, and they help others learn and own their choices.
Sisters of Code is not only about growing digital skills, it’s confidence in a young woman’s voice, ambition in her plans, and dignity in her choices. This program is not only about learning to use technology, but about raising a new generation of Cambodian girls who are ready to lead, create, and shape the future. Sisters of Code tells them, clearly and loudly: we see you, we believe in you, and you belong. To reach more girls, we invite you to join us. The time for positive change is now. Choose a future where everyone feels they belong.
Mrs. Dalin CHIN
Project Leader
I truly believe that every girl, no matter where she comes from, deserves the opportunity to explore technology with confidence. As Cambodia’s digital future continues to grow, we need more girls to step forward and be part of shaping it knowing that their voice truly matters.
I am pleased and honored to support Sisters of Code’s mission to grow into a nationwide movement that supports girls not only in learning digital skills, but also in becoming creators, innovators, and future leaders in Cambodia’s digital economy.
Ms. Mab MY
Project Manager
I am proud to be part of the Sisters of Code community, where women support women and young girls are welcomed to explore technology freely and safely. If you are curious about tech, know that you belong here. With the right guidance and encouragement, every Cambodian girl has the potential to learn, grow, and succeed in technology.
Ms. Lauren SONG
Project Manager
Working for Sisters of Code has been a privilege, as it allows me to implement programs that directly serve girls and women across Cambodia. This work reminds me of the importance of creating inclusive spaces where girls and women can build strong digital skills and gain confidence to study and work in the tech sector. As technology advances at a rapid pace, it is reshaping both education and the workforce and reinforcing the need for a concerted effort to strengthen human capital to meet the growing demand for a digitally literate and highly skilled workforce.
Trainers’ Messages
Mrs. Vapy OEURN
My name is Oeurn Vapy, and I am an Information Technology teacher at Preah Sisowath High School under the New Generation School Program. My journey as a trainer began with a deep belief in STEM education as a powerful tool to unlock students’ curiosity, creativity, and problem-solving skills. Since joining Sisters of Code in 2021, I have witnessed both the challenges and the untapped potential of girls in technology. Despite their abilities, women and girls remain underrepresented in the IT field, especially at higher education levels.
​
This reality motivates me to actively promote tech education for girls and to support them in building confidence, skills, and ambition. Technology creates opportunities, not only for employment, but for innovation and independence. Through Sisters of Code, I am proud to help inspire the next generation of female creators and leaders.
To all women: believe in yourself, support one another, and know that technology belongs to you too.
Mrs. Mithona KIM
Working with girls at the Sisters of Code Club has been an inspiring experience. As a trainer, I’ve seen how a supportive and inclusive learning environment helps girls build confidence in technology and believe in their abilities.
​
One of the most rewarding experiences is watching students move from hesitation to curiosity, and then to confidently solving problems on their own. Their creativity and persistence often lead to innovative solutions and thoughtful questions.
​
The club doesn’t just teach technical skills, it builds teamwork, leadership, and a growth mindset. Training these girls has reaffirmed my belief that early mentorship and encouragement can truly shape the future of women in technology.
Ms. Phallideth PHEN
When I began my university studies in a technology-related major, I was motivated yet uncertain. Entering a field where the majority of students were male, I often questioned whether I had made the right academic choice.  My perspective changed when I joined Sisters of Code. Sisters of Code was the first place where I felt truly supported, both technically and emotionally. I connected with young women who shared similar interests and challenges. This environment played a critical role in stabilizing my mindset and reinforcing my commitment to the technology field.
​
Following the program, I continued my involvement by becoming a Sisters of Code Ambassador. I led an 18-week coding club for high school girls. I blended both theory and hands-on exercises so that students understand coding concepts. I used tools like code.org and Scratch for students to create interactive games, animations, and digital storytelling projects. Watching them build, experiment, and gain confidence reminded me why representation matters.
​
Through these experiences, I was selected for the Women in STEM Scholarship to pursue a master’s degree in the UK. That opportunity was not just a personal achievement, it was proof that belief, support, and community can change lives.
​
Today, I remain actively engaged with Sisters of Code as a trainer, delivering personal development and work-readiness programs, and advocating for greater female participation in the technology sector. I am forever grateful to be part of the Sisters of Code community. It didn’t just teach me how to code, but it taught me to believe in myself.

Sisters of Code and Amret Launch “Riel Sisters” Financial Literacy Course for Young Women in Cambodia
Sisters of Code
Oct 16
4 min read
Riel Sisters
, a digital and financial literacy initiative by
Sisters of Code
, has been selected by
MIT Solve
as a winner of the
Bank SinoPac Ltd.
Prize for Innovation in Southeast Asia
.
The initiative is part of the
Digital Finance Basics for Girls in Southeast Asia
project, implemented by Sisters of Code in partnership with
Amret
, with support from
MIT Solve
and funding from
Bank SinoPac Ltd.
This selection is an important recognition of Sisters of Code’s work in Cambodia, building on our selection as a MIT Solve Solver team in 2020. It expands our digital education programs to include practical financial skills that young women can use throughout their lives.
Working with Amret, Sisters of Code will launch the course in late November for
100-150 female high-school and first-year university students
. The collaboration reflects Amret’s commitment to investing in young people’s skills and financial confidence as a foundation for a more inclusive and sustainable future.
Training is planned in Phnom Penh, with partnerships being developed to bring the course to students in the provinces. Reaching young women beyond the capital is a priority for the project.
Why financial literacy matters for young women
Starting university or a first job often means managing money more independently. Young women may need to budget for transport, meals, rent and study costs while learning to use a bank account or banking app.
Learning to plan spending, understand interest rates and borrowing, and build disciplined, mindful money habits gives young women useful skills for life. These skills can help them manage their income, prepare for unexpected expenses and work towards their goals.
Women run roughly six in ten businesses in Cambodia, including many market stalls, small shops and microenterprises. Financial skills matter for their livelihoods and for the next generation preparing to earn and manage their own money.
World Bank Global Findex data from 2021, cited by Women’s World Banking, show that 34% of Cambodian women had borrowed from a formal financial institution in the previous year, compared with 28% of men. Yet only 4% of women had saved money in an account, compared with 10% of men. These figures highlight a gap between the use of credit and formal savings.
“Riel Sisters” gives students an opportunity to practise financial decisions in a supportive learning environment and build confidence in managing their own money.
“Riel Sisters” for real needs
“Riel Sisters” course is designed for students with limited or no experience in banking, budgeting and digital financial tools. Training will be delivered in Khmer, with English financial terms introduced to help students understand the vocabulary used in apps and financial documents.
Across four sessions of 2.5 hours each delivered on the weekends, students will explore:
Money and digital safety:
Understand Cambodia’s financial system, check financial providers and secure their phones and banking apps.
Budgeting and saving:
Record spending, distinguish needs from wants, build a personal finance tracker in Google Sheets and set a realistic savings goal.
Payments and borrowing:
Practice checking KHQR payments using demonstration screens, understand interest and fees, and compare the total cost of loans and installment plans.
Scam awareness:
Identify warning signs in suspicious calls, messages and offers, and practise responding with “Stop, Check, Ask.”
Students will work in pairs and teams, take part in games and complete short activities between sessions. They might track a week of spending, calculate the full cost of an advertised loan or spot an incorrect recipient name in a payment example.
Tools and habits students can keep
Each participant will finish with a personal finance tracker, a savings goal and a one-page financial plan. She will also receive a pocket card with eight practical Money Rules covering spending, saving, borrowing and digital safety.
The aim is to help students put what they learn into daily practice: recording expenses, setting money aside where possible, checking costs before committing and protecting their PINs and one-time passwords.
Participants will also be encouraged to share one Money Rule with a family member, taking useful knowledge beyond the classroom.
Sisters of Code and Amret’s partnership
Sisters of Code, a non-profit educational program by IT Academy STEP Institute, leads the course design and delivery. Sisters of Code Ambassadors will be trained to facilitate the sessions, bringing their experience in teaching digital skills and supporting younger students.
Amret represents Bank SinoPac in Cambodia and contributes financial content expertise and a guest session on saving, borrowing and understanding financial products. This would support the quality of the training and real life experiences from the experts.
The training will focus on helping students compare options and make informed decisions. Payment exercises will use demonstration screens, with no real money transferred in class. Students will not be asked to disclose account balances, PINs or family debts.
Bringing financial education to the provinces
Reaching students beyond the capital is a priority for “Riel Sisters”. Alongside training in Phnom Penh, we will work to establish partnerships that bring the course closer to young women in the provinces.
The course is designed for both in-person and online delivery, giving us more ways to reach students in different locations. Local partnerships will help us organise access to training and the digital tools students need for practical activities.

On 27 September 2026,
Mrs. CHIN Dalin, Project Leader
at
Sisters of Code
, was invited by
UN Women Cambodia
to share her experience working with young women in technology at the
Youth Dialogue: “Empowering Youth for Women, Peace, and Security through Online Safety and Inclusive Digital Spaces.”
The dialogue was organized by UN Women Cambodia and co-designed with youth groups. It brought together
86 participants
, including representatives from government ministries and public institutions, youth-led organizations, and UN agencies.
The dialogue focused on strengthening young people's awareness of the
Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda
, including emerging non-traditional security issues such as cybersecurity and climate security, promoting responsible online engagement, and highlighting the important role of youth in contributing to policy discussions.
H.E. Koung Sorita, Secretary of State at the Ministry of Women's Affairs
Ms. Vladanka Andreeva, UN Resident Coordinator in Cambodia
Ms. Bridget Collier, Deputy Head of Mission at the Australian Embassy in Cambodia
Sisters of Code at UN Women in Cambodia's Youth Dialogue 2026
For Sisters of Code, the dialogue provided an important opportunity to bring young women's experiences into the conversation around digital safety and inclusion.
From digital access to digital confidence
Mrs. Chin Dalin, Project Leader for Sisters of Code
Empowering young women in digital spaces means giving them not only access to technology, but also the skills and confidence to navigate it safely.
Sharing from her experience at Sisters of Code, Mrs. CHIN Dalin posed a simple but important question:
“If we teach a girl how to code, use AI, and build her own website, but never teach her how to protect the account where all her work is stored, can we really say that we have prepared her for the digital world?”
Since joining Sisters of Code in 2024, Mrs. CHIN Dalin has worked alongside the team to support girls and young women in developing digital and technology skills.
Sisters of Code provides free digital education and technology skills development for girls across Cambodia. Its programmes go beyond coding to include areas such as digital skills, artificial intelligence, online safety, teamwork, and leadership.
The goal is not only to help girls become technology users, but also to become digital creators and confident participants in the digital world.
However, as Sisters of Code continues working directly with young learners, one important lesson has become increasingly clear:
Before young women can fully participate in the digital world, they also need to know how to protect themselves within it.
What are girls experiencing online?
To better understand these experiences, Sisters of Code conducted an online safety survey in September 2026 with
133 students
, most of whom were between the ages of 10 and 20.
The survey is not intended to represent all Cambodian girls and young women, as Sisters of Code students are already an active group of technology users. Nevertheless, their responses provide valuable insight into the online experiences and concerns of young women participating in digital learning.
Most students reported using the internet every day, particularly for
learning, communication, and social media
.
Sisters of Code's Online Safety Survey Results 2026
At the same time, they are exposed to a range of online risks. The most frequently reported concerns were
online scams and account theft or loss
.
Sisters of Code's Online Safety Survey Results 2026
Even though online bullying and strangers contacting me are not in the top concerns by the Sisters of Code students, the findings still deserve the attention:
1 in 3 students
reported experiencing or facing online bullying or harassment.
1 in 4 students
said that strangers had contacted them online.
Only
10%
reported that they had never experienced any of the listed online threats.
Sisters of Code's Online Safety Survey Results 2026
These findings highlight an important reality:
being connected brings challenges and risks of online safety.
Continuous training and awareness building
Sisters of Code's Online Safety Survey Results 2026
The survey, which presented views of female students who are active digitally, showed that continuous efforts are required to update skills and awareness.
Only
6%
gave themselves the highest confidence rating.
Sisters of Code's Online Safety Survey Results 2026
Meanwhile,
66% were not sure that they had sufficient skills to protect themselves online.
For Sisters of Code, this finding reinforces the importance of combining digital inclusion with practical online safety education.
Young people need more than general awareness. They need practical skills that they can apply in their everyday digital lives, including how to:
Create strong and secure passwords.
Recognize scams and suspicious messages.
Respond when an account is hacked or compromised.
Protect personal information and privacy.
Report online bullying and abuse.
Seek support when facing online threats rather than dealing with them alone.
These skills are essential for helping young people participate in digital spaces with greater confidence and awareness.
Online safety is also about well-being and freedom
As part of the survey, Sisters of Code asked students what “online safety” meant to them.
One response described online safety as protecting personal information, privacy, accounts, and devices from scams, account hacking, and online harassment—while being able to use the internet
with confidence and without fear
.
The phrase
“without fear”
stood out.
Online safety is not only a technical issue. It is also connected to
peace of mind, confidence, well-being, and freedom to participate
.
When a young woman feels safe online, she can be more willing to ask questions, share ideas, create, collaborate, and take on leadership roles.
This is particularly relevant to the broader Women, Peace and Security agenda, where meaningful participation and inclusion are central. Creating inclusive digital spaces means ensuring that young women can participate in those spaces without being pushed away by harassment, threats, or fear.
Four areas for stronger online safety education
Based on the survey findings, Sisters of Code identified four key areas where digital safety education can help young women better protect themselves:
1. Technical Protection:
Supporting young people to protect their accounts, devices, and passwords.
2. Threat Detection:
Building the ability to identify phishing, scams, fraudulent messages, and AI-generated fake content.
3. Data Protection:
Strengthening understanding of privacy, personal information, and responses to digital harassment.
4. Financial Safety:
Helping young people safely navigate digital money, online payments, and related financial risks.
Sisters of Code's Online Safety Survey Results 2026
These areas demonstrate why online safety should not be treated as an optional topic or something young people learn only after experiencing a problem.
Online safety should be an essential component of digital literacy education.
Integrating these skills into digital learning can help young people strengthen their awareness, confidence, well-being, and ability to respond to potential threats.
Youth are part of the solution
The Youth Dialogue also emphasized the important role of young people in advancing the Women, Peace and Security agenda and contributing to policy discussions.
For Sisters of Code, young people should not be viewed only as beneficiaries of digital education. They are also
active contributors to conversations about the digital future
.
They are already navigating online spaces every day. They understand the opportunities, experience the challenges, and can help identify the knowledge and support they need.
Listening to young people therefore means more than inviting them to participate in discussions. It means creating meaningful opportunities for them to
share their experiences, shape solutions, and contribute to decisions that affect their digital lives.
Digital inclusion must include digital safety
Through her sharing at the UN Women Youth Dialogue, Mrs. CHIN Dalin emphasized the central message of Sisters of Code's work:
“Digital inclusion must include digital safety.” She continued “When we navigate safely in the world of technology, it is a key to building inclusive and empowering world where women are creators of their future”
Opening the door to technology is only the beginning. Girls and young women also need the skills, confidence, and support to walk through that door safely.
The digital world can be compared to a vast ocean. We cannot encourage young people to explore it without also giving them the knowledge and tools they need to navigate safely.
For Sisters of Code, the goal is therefore not simply to see more girls and young women online. It is to see them become safe, informed, confident, empowered, and active participants in the digital world—young women who can learn, create, lead, and contribute without fear.
Because true digital inclusion is not only about having access to technology.
It is about having the confidence and safety to use that access to create a better future.

Sisters of Code and EBC Organization Sign MOU to Expand Access to Digital Education
Sisters of Code
Jul 10
2 min read
On July 9, 2026,
Sisters of Code
officially signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with
Educational Broadcasting Cambodia (EBC)
Organization to expand access to quality digital education for female students across Cambodia.
The partnership focuses on jointly developing digital and coding educational content, establishing a learning management system (LMS) on EBC's platforms, and expanding learning opportunities for Sisters of Code female students at
Community Tech Centers
in Takeo Province and beyond. This initiative is supported through the funding of the Capacity Building Research and Development (CBRD) program of the
Ministry of Post and Telecommunications.
Mr. Se Mouthycheat & Mrs. Natalja Rodionova
The MOU was signed by
Mr. Se Mouthycheat
, President of EBC Organization, and
Mrs. Natalja Rodionova
, Founder of Sisters of Code and Managing Director of
IT Academy STEP Cambodia Institut
e
, in the presence of representatives from both organizations.
This collaboration marks an important milestone in creating a more innovative, inclusive, and accessible learning ecosystem for Cambodian students, particularly those living outside Phnom Penh. Through EBC's digital learning platforms, hundreds of Sisters of Code students will be able to access high-quality coding and digital skills lessons anytime and anywhere, making learning more flexible and accessible.
Mr. Se Mouthycheat (left)
During the meeting,
Mr. Se Mouthycheat
highlighted EBC's ongoing efforts to make education more accessible. Thousands of educational videos are already available on EBC's online platforms, allowing learners across Cambodia to study independently at their own pace. This approach responds to the growing demand for online and self-directed learning while helping equip Cambodian youth with the digital skills needed for the future workforce.
Mrs. Natalja Rodionova (right)
Mrs. Natalja Rodionova
expressed her sincere appreciation to Mr. Se Mouthycheat and the EBC team for their dedication to producing educational content that benefits Cambodian students nationwide. She also thanked EBC for its commitment to supporting Sisters of Code's mission of empowering girls with digital and coding skills.
Since its establishment, Sisters of Code has remained committed to bridging the gender gap in digital skills by providing free digital education for girls in a safe and supportive learning environment. Through this partnership with EBC Organization, Sisters of Code is taking another significant step forward by making its learning opportunities more inclusive, innovative, and accessible to students regardless of where they live.
Together, Sisters of Code and EBC Organization share a common vision of expanding equitable access to quality digital education for students across Cambodia, regardless of their background or location.
We look forward with great enthusiasm to the positive impact this partnership will bring.

. Funded by the

Mrs. Natalja Rodionova

Mrs. Natalja Rodionova

. As the founder, Mrs. Natalja believes that girls and women can thrive in the digital technology sector when given the right opportunities and quality education. agreed the program helped improve their professional skills.

Sisters of Code Ambassadors 2026 Graduation
Sisters of Code
May 12
4 min read
On the morning of May 10, 2026,
Sisters of Code
was delighted to organized a graduation ceremony to celebrate
65 female students
who have successfully completed the
Sisters of Code Ambassadors Program 2026
.
Sisters of Code Ambassadors 2026 Graduation
The ceremony began with a warm welcome speech from
Mrs. Natalja Rodionova
, Founder of
Sisters of Code
and Managing Director at
IT Academy STEP Cambodia Institute
.
Mrs. Natalja Rodionova
Founded in 2019, Sisters of Code started as a small initiative with a mission to empower girls in Cambodia to learn technology. Today, the community has grown to
more than 1,000 students,
many of whom continue to learn, participate, and take leadership roles in Cambodia’s growing technology sector.
During her speech, Mrs. Natalja shared her belief that girls should — and can — play an important role in shaping the future of digital technology. She also reflected that the celebration of 65 successful graduates is a meaningful sign that more girls are becoming interested in technology, highlighting the importance of continuing to build a supportive, safe, and inclusive environment where girls can learn, grow, and fully unleash their potential.
Ms. My Mab
According to the final survey completed by 59 students, 100% reported that they gained a better understanding of coding, developed new digital skills, and felt more confident in using those skills.
As presented by
Ms. My Mab
, Project Manager for Sisters of Code, all students also expressed interest in joining other Sisters of Code programs in the future. In addition, 100% said they would recommend Sisters of Code educational programs to other girls as well.
Sisters of Code trainers,
Ms. Phen Phallideth
and
Ms. Chao Chealy
, also joined the ceremony and shared heartfelt messages with the students. “I became emotional on the last day of class,” said Ms. Phallideth. She continued, “I’m used to teaching you all every weekend. Now that the class has ended, I already miss those moments. But I’m also very happy to see my students successfully graduate from this intensive program.” Ms. Chealy also shared, “I’m most proud to see my students persist through challenges and make it to graduation today.”
Sisters of Code is deeply grateful to our trainers who dedicate their weekends to teaching girls and equipping them with digital skills that help prepare them to become confident and capable digital citizens.
During the ceremony, two students also took turns delivering short presentations on their journey with the Sisters of Code Ambassadors Program 2026.
Ms. Dy Pichpenhboromey
Ms. Dy Pichpenhboromey
, Sisters of Code Ambassadors 2026, shared that she did not initially receive support to pursue a technology major. However, after learning about Sisters of Code, joining the program, and connecting with female trainers and peers, she began to feel encouraged to pursue a field often seen as male-dominated.
Ms. Noung Mouy
Ms. Noung Mouy
, Sisters of Code Ambassadors 2026, ended her presentation with a powerful message: “Girls are not just girls, they are creators, changemakers, and leaders who shape the future.” Ms. Mouy also highlighted the skills she gained from the 15-week program, including basic coding, game development, website development, and fundamentals of AI, as well as leadership and public speaking skills.
Out of 65 graduates from the Sisters of Code Ambassadors Program this year,
22 students
have been selected as Sisters of Code Clubs Leaders for 2026. This marks an important milestone in their journey from learners to leaders, as they now step forward to share their knowledge and inspire other girls who are curious and passionate about technology.
Sisters of Code warmly congratulated them on this achievement. To recognize their dedication and growth, Mrs. Natalja presented each of them with a traditional Krama as a token of appreciation and encouragement as they begin their new leadership role.
Sisters of Code Clubs Leaders 2026
The recognition did not stop there. Out of 65 graduates, four students were named Top Students of their cohort:
Ms. Sam Leak Proapey, Ms. Toek Chhunhor, Ms. Pheak Sotheara,
and
Ms. Van Sokkeang.
Top Students in the Sisters of Code Ambassadors Program 2026
They stood out for their consistent commitment throughout the program, strong attendance, and exceptional final projects, based on evaluations from our trainers. In appreciation of their excellent performance, Top Student awards were presented to all four students.
The celebration continued as Sisters of Code presented certificates of completion to all 65 graduates. Each student received a certificate from Sisters of Code, and those who joined the Work Readiness Program also received an additional certificate from Deloitte Cambodia, a long-standing partner of Sisters of Code in the Ambassadors Program.
Mrs. Chin Dalin
As the ceremony came to a close,
Mrs. Chin Dalin
, Project Leader for Sisters of Code, took the stage to deliver the final remarks. She extended heartfelt appreciation to the students for their commitment despite challenges, to the trainers for dedicating their weekends to teaching, to the Sisters of Code team for ensuring a safe and supportive learning environment, and to Deloitte Cambodia for providing training sessions that prepare students for future employment opportunities. Mrs. Dalin also highlighted the important role of parents in supporting their daughters to pursue learning in technology.
The program then moved into a cake-cutting moment, followed by a warm time of celebration, photos, and refreshments shared together.
At its heart, this graduation is more than a closing ceremony. It reflects the Sisters of Code mission to create safe and inclusive spaces where girls can explore technology, build confidence, and grow into future creators and leaders. With the continued support of families, trainers, and partners, we remain committed to empowering more girls to believe in their potential and shape their own future in tech.
